title: Secure passwords
subtitle: Better logins in 10 minutes
description: Passwords protect your accounts and data, and those of your team. In this course you will learn what makes a password strong, how to remember lots of passwords and what to do if a password falls into the wrong hands.

objectives.text: You can explain what makes a password strong.
You can create a strong, memorable password using the sentence method.
You can take the right steps if a password has been compromised.

chapters.title: What makes a password strong
chapters.intro: Attackers don’t guess passwords by hand — they try millions of combinations per second.

blocks.body:
During an attack, a computer systematically tries every possible combination. Each extra character **multiplies** the number of possibilities.

That is why **length beats complexity**. A 16-character password is far more secure than an 8-character one full of special characters.

image.alt: A shield with a padlock above a row of password dots.

blocks.body: Use at least **14 characters**. The longer, the better.

items.title: Strong
items.body:
- at least 14 characters long
- unique for every account
- contains no personal details
- not found in dictionaries or leak lists

items.title: Weak
items.body:
- short, e.g. ‘Summer24!’
- used more than once
- contains names, dates of birth or pets
- follows a pattern such as ‘Password1’, ‘Password2’ …

cards.back: An attack that automatically tries **every combination**.
Attackers test leaked login details **on other services**. So never reuse passwords.
A program that creates **unique passwords** and stores them encrypted.

question.prompt: Which password is the most secure?

feedback.correct: It is long, contains no personal details and is still easy to remember.
feedback.incorrect: Focus above all on **length** and on avoiding personal details.

blocks.body: With the sentence method you can create a long password in seconds that is still easy to remember.

items.title: Think of a sentence
items.body: Think of a sentence only you know, e.g. ‘On Monday I cycle 12 km to the office’.

items.title: Take the first letters
items.body: Take the first letters and numbers: **OMIc12kttO**.

items.title: Make it longer
items.body: Add a separator and another word until you have at least 14 characters.

items.title: Save it in a password manager
items.body: For all other accounts, let the password manager create a random password.

items.title: Do I need to change my passwords regularly?
items.body: No. Only change a password if it might have been compromised. Frequent changes often lead to weaker passwords.

items.title: Can I write my passwords down?
items.body: Not on notes stuck to your screen. Use a password manager instead.

pages.title: When a password has been leaked

blocks.title: A suspicious message
blocks.situation: You receive an automated email: the password for one of your private online accounts was found in a data leak. You use the same password for your work account.

choices.text: I ignore the email — it’s bound to be spam.
choices.feedback: Risky. Check the warning on the service’s official website, not via links in the email. If it is genuine, attackers already have your password.

choices.text: I only change the password of my private account.
choices.feedback: A good first step, but not enough. Because you reuse the password, your work account is also at risk.

choices.text: I change the password wherever I have used it and report the incident to IT.
choices.feedback: This closes every gap, and IT can check whether there have already been suspicious logins.

blocks.title: If in doubt
blocks.body: Report a possible password leak to IT **immediately** — even if you are not sure.

items: Length beats complexity: at least 14 characters.
A separate password for every account.
The sentence method helps you remember long passwords.
After a leak: change it everywhere and inform IT.

quiz.title: Final quiz
quiz.intro: Test your knowledge. You can retake the quiz as often as you like.

questions.prompt: A password with 8 characters and lots of special characters is more secure than one with 16 lower-case letters.

feedback.incorrect: Length matters more than special characters.

questions.explanation: Length increases the number of possible combinations more than extra special characters do.

questions.prompt: Which features does a strong password have?

options.text: It is at least 14 characters long.
It is only used for one account.
It contains your date of birth so you can remember it.

feedback.correct: Length and uniqueness are what count.
feedback.incorrect: Check which features really protect against attacks.

questions.explanation: Length and uniqueness are decisive. Personal details are easy to guess, and frequent changes often lead to weaker passwords.

questions.prompt: Which password was created correctly with the sentence method?

options.text: Mldi2kh-Sunrise (from ‘My little dog is 2 kilos heavy’)

feedback.correct: The password is based on a personal sentence and has been lengthened.
feedback.incorrect: Remember the four steps of the sentence method.

questions.explanation: The sentence method uses the first letters of a personal sentence and lengthens them if necessary.

questions.prompt: Your sentence password only has 11 characters. What do you do?

options.text: Add a separator and another word.
Add an exclamation mark at the end.

feedback.correct: That is a quick way to reach the length you need.
feedback.incorrect: Remember the minimum length of 14 characters.

questions.explanation: An extra word makes the password much longer and is still easy to remember.

questions.prompt: Match the terms with their descriptions.

pairs.right: Leaked login details are tested on other services.

feedback.incorrect: Have another look at the term cards in chapter 1.

questions.prompt: Your password has been leaked and you also use it for your work account. What do you do?

options.text: Wait and see whether anything happens.
Change the password everywhere and inform IT.

feedback.incorrect: Remember that you use the password more than once.

questions.explanation: Change the password wherever you have used it and report the incident to IT.

questions.prompt: You only report a possible password leak to IT once you are sure it is genuine.

feedback.correct: Exactly — better to report once too often.

questions.explanation: IT can only react quickly if it is informed early — even if it is only a suspicion.
